lesson_title: Purple Cabbage Water Is a Chemistry Spy
hook_text: Boil some red cabbage, pour off the purple water, and you have made a chemistry detector.
clip_script: Water, vinegar and cleaning liquid can all look exactly the same. Tasting to find out is dangerous. So scientists use colour spies called indicators. Litmus paper comes in red and blue. Acid turns blue paper red. Base turns red paper blue. Neutral changes nothing. Blue to red, acid instead; red to blue, base for you. You need both strips, or you cannot spot a neutral. Now make your own spy. Soak chopped red cabbage in hot water until it goes purple. Add vinegar: pink. Plain water: stays purple. Baking soda: blue, then green. Its colours even hint at how strong the acid or base is. Bonus: turmeric turns red with soap, which is why curry stains blush in the wash.
visual_style: Whiteboard litmus strips flipping colour beside labelled cups; a purple cabbage jug pouring into three glasses that turn pink, purple and green; a yellow curry stain turning red.
pacing: Quick litmus rules, a slow satisfying colour pour, a cheeky turmeric finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and test your kitchen with cabbage water.
